questions.question: State the distance, midpoint and gradient formulae, and apply all three to A(−3; 2) and B(5; 8), showing your working.
questions.expected_answer: Distance: the square root of (x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)². Midpoint: ((x₁ + x₂)/2 ; (y₁ + y₂)/2). Gradient: (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). For A(−3; 2) and B(5; 8): the change in x is 5 − (−3) = 8 and the change in y is 8 − 2 = 6. Distance AB = √(8² + 6²) = √(64 + 36) = √100 = 10 units. Midpoint = ((−3 + 5)/2 ; (2 + 8)/2) = (1; 5). Gradient = 6/8 = 3/4, meaning the line climbs 3 units for every 4 units across. Note that the midpoint formula is the only one of the three that adds the coordinates; distance and gradient both subtract.

questions.question: Explain the four possible cases for the gradient of a line, and state the conditions for two lines to be parallel and for two lines to be perpendicular, including where the perpendicular test breaks down.
questions.expected_answer: A positive gradient means the line rises from left to right; a negative gradient means it falls from left to right; a gradient of zero means the line is horizontal, because the change in y is zero; and a vertical line has an undefined gradient, because the change in x is zero and division by zero has no meaning — undefined is not the same as zero. Two lines are parallel when their gradients are equal. Two lines are perpendicular when the product of their gradients is −1, equivalently when one gradient is the negative reciprocal of the other: 3/4 pairs with −4/3, and 3/4 × (−4/3) = −1. The test breaks down for a horizontal and a vertical line, which are perpendicular but have gradients of zero and undefined, so no product exists; that pair must be handled by inspection.

questions.question: For A(−3; 2), B(5; 8), C(9; 3) and D(1; −3), prove that ABCD is a parallelogram and explain why it is neither a rectangle nor a rhombus.
questions.expected_answer: Side lengths: AB = √(8² + 6²) = 10 and CD = √((−8)² + (−6)²) = 10; BC = √(4² + (−5)²) = √41 and DA = √((−4)² + 5²) = √41. Both pairs of opposite sides are equal, which is a condition for a parallelogram. Gradients confirm it: gradient AB = 6/8 = 3/4 and gradient DC = 6/8 = 3/4, so AB ∥ DC; gradient AD = −5/4 and gradient BC = −5/4, so AD ∥ BC. A third proof: the midpoint of AC is (3; 2,5) and the midpoint of BD is (3; 2,5), so the diagonals bisect each other. It is not a rectangle because gradient AB × gradient AD = 3/4 × (−5/4) = −15/16, which is not −1, so angle A is not a right angle. It is not a rhombus because the four sides are not all equal: 10 does not equal √41. ABCD is therefore a parallelogram and nothing more.
